title: Improper integrals and independent limiting operations
terms: improper integral; unbounded interval; endpoint singularity; interior singularity; con- vergent improper integral; divergent improper integral; Cauchy principal value; improper integral of the first kind; improper integral of the second kind; absolute convergence of an improper integral; conditional convergence of an improper integral.

Symmetric cancellation is not ordinary convergence: a Cauchy principal value may exist when
the improper integral diverges. Split at every singularity and verify each piece before adding.
A substitution may simplify evaluation, but does not waive convergence checks. Finite interval
length does not guarantee convergence when the integrand blows up, and an infinite interval
does not force divergence if decay is sufficient.
An improper integral is absolutely convergent if the integral of the absolute value is finite. It
is conditionally convergent if the original improper integral converges but the absolute-value
integral does not. Oscillation can produce conditional convergence on one infinite tail, which is
different from cancelling two independently divergent tails by a principal value.
An infinite limit of integration makes an integral improper of the first kind. An unbounded
integrand at a finite endpoint or an interior point makes it improper of the second kind. Both
causes can occur together and must each be handled by a separate limiting check.

solution.text:
Integrate the difference [1/(x + a) − 1/(x + b)]/(b − a) over [0, R]. The upper boundary is
log[(R + a)/(R + b)]/(b − a) → 0; the lower boundary is log(a/b)/(b − a). Their difference
gives the answer. The two partial fractions must be combined before taking the infinite
limit; their separate divergent integrals cannot be subtracted.
